sections.heading: Coming to you as your justified child
sections.text: Heavenly Father, save me completely from sin. I know my right standing with you is not something I earned; it rests on the righteousness of Jesus, given to me. But I do not want only to be forgiven while staying unlike you. I long to resemble you. I am your child, so make the family likeness visible in me.
theological_themes: Justification by the righteousness of Christ, not personal merit
Desire for holiness and conformity to God's image

scripture_references.connection: Paul grounds the believer's righteousness in Christ's sin-bearing work, not in the believer's own moral record. This supports the prayer's confidence that acceptance with God comes through another's righteousness.
This passage describes believers as adopted children of God who cry out to him as Father. It fits the prayer's movement from secure sonship to the desire to bear the Father's likeness.
Paul says God's saving purpose includes conforming believers to the image of his Son. That gives biblical shape to the longing not merely to be pardoned, but to become like Christ.

sections.heading: Asking to be free from sin's grip
sections.text: Help me understand, deep down, that in Christ I have died to sin. When sin calls for my attention, make me unwilling to listen. Do not only free me from sin when it has already taken over; protect me from its first entrance into my desires, my thoughts, and my choices.
theological_themes: Union with Christ in death to sin
Freedom from both the rule and intrusion of sin

scripture_references.connection: Paul tells believers to consider themselves dead to sin and alive to God, and not to let sin reign in their bodies. This directly supports the prayer's plea to recognize death to sin and be delivered from its dominion.
James traces sin from desire to action to death, showing why the prayer asks for help before sin gains ground. The danger begins inwardly, not only after outward failure.

sections.heading: Learning to walk in Christ's life
sections.text: Teach me to walk the way Jesus walked. Let his risen life shape my ordinary life: a life of love, a life of faith, a life that is clean and set apart for you. Do not let holiness remain an idea I admire; make it the path I actually take today.
theological_themes: Love, faith, and holiness as marks of Christian living

scripture_references.connection: John says that whoever abides in Christ ought to walk as Jesus walked. This grounds the prayer's request for a life patterned after Christ rather than merely associated with him in name.
Paul connects union with Christ's resurrection to walking in newness of life. The prayer's desire for a new life of love, faith, and holiness flows from that resurrection reality.
Believers are called to imitate God as beloved children and walk in love as Christ loved us. This ties together childlike identity and Christlike love in daily conduct.

sections.heading: Confessing the sins I hate in myself
sections.text: Father, I hate the deadness that still clings to me: my laziness, envy, smallness of spirit, and pride. Forgive me, and do not merely cover these sins—put them to death in me. Have mercy on my unbelief, on my crooked desires, and on my heart when it wanders from you.
theological_themes: Need for help with unbelief and a wandering heart

scripture_references.connection: Paul's cry over the 'body of death' expresses the believer's anguish over remaining sin while looking to Christ for deliverance. It closely matches the prayer's grief over inward corruption.
Paul commands believers to put to death earthly sins and put on the new self. This supports the prayer's request not only for pardon, but for the killing of specific vices.
The father's plea, 'help my unbelief,' gives biblical language for asking God to have mercy on mixed faith. The prayer similarly admits real trust in God alongside remaining unbelief.

sections.heading: Receiving your gifts without making idols of them
sections.text: When your blessings come, I often start clinging to the gift as if it were my god. I can give my heart to children, friends, money, reputation, or anything else I love. Cleanse me from that unfaithfulness. Teach me to love your gifts rightly, without giving them your place. Keep my deepest affection for you.
theological_themes: Ordering loves under love for God

scripture_references.connection: James uses the language of spiritual adultery for divided loyalty toward God. That supports the prayer's confession that misplaced ultimate affection is not harmless preference but covenant unfaithfulness.

Jesus teaches that even the closest family loves must not outrank love for him. This clarifies the prayer's concern: not that people should be loved less than rightly, but that no created good should take God's place.

John's closing command to keep away from idols addresses more than carved images; it warns believers against anything that competes with God for trust and devotion. This fits the prayer's concern over turning blessings into rivals.

sections.heading: Letting your victory show in my life
sections.text: Sin is the worst thing in me and the worst thing for me. Let Christ's victory become real to my conscience and visible in the way I live. Make me devoted to you, steady in trust, ready to obey, willing to yield, and childlike in my confidence in you.
theological_themes: Sin as the believer's deepest enemy
Assurance expressed in obedience and trust

scripture_references.connection: God's grace saves and also trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live devoted lives while Christ purifies a people for himself. This connects inner assurance of grace with outward transformation.

Paul thanks God for victory through Jesus Christ and then calls believers to steadfast, fruitful living. That pattern matches the prayer's desire for Christ's victory to be both inwardly known and outwardly displayed.

sections.heading: Changing my love, my speech, and my daily character
sections.text: Teach me to love you with all my heart, soul, mind, and strength, and to love my neighbor as myself. Rescue me from an unchanged temper, suspicious thoughts, cutting words, cheap attitudes, and unkind ways. Put a guard over my mouth. Help me master my tongue instead of being mastered by it. Fill me with grace every day, so that what comes out of my life is clean, steady, and life-giving.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus summarizes God's commands as wholehearted love for God and love for neighbor. This directly grounds the prayer's request for rightly ordered love in both devotion and relationships.
The psalmist asks God to guard his mouth and keep watch over his lips. This supports the prayer's dependence on God for mastery over speech rather than relying on self-control alone.

James exposes the contradiction of blessing God while harming people with the tongue, using the image of fresh and bitter water. This illuminates the prayer's request that the whole life become like a fountain of clean water.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses the phrase 'spiritual adultery' for misplaced affection toward blessings such as children, friends, wealth, and honor. This is biblically grounded language, but it can be pastorally misunderstood as a rejection of human loves rather than a warning against making them ultimate.

The original asks God to 'close my heart to all but thee.' Rendered woodenly, this could seem to contradict the prayer's later request to love one's neighbor. The adaptation clarifies that God should hold the supreme place while his gifts are loved rightly under him.
significant_interpretive_choices: 'Righteous through the righteousness of another' was rendered explicitly as the righteousness of Jesus given to the believer, because the prayer assumes classic Protestant justification by Christ's righteousness.

'Deliver me from the invasion as well as the dominion of sin' was interpreted as asking for protection from sin's early entrance into desires and thoughts, not only rescue after outward sin has become habitual.
'Body of death' was kept conceptually rather than quoted, with specific vices named, to preserve the Puritan sense of grief over remaining sin without relying on archaic phrasing.
'Chastity' was interpreted spiritually as undivided covenant loyalty to God, not merely sexual purity, because the surrounding lines concern idolatrous attachment to blessings.
